title: Improved screening of doped ZrO$_2$ catalysts for CO$_2$ hydrogenation from graph-based machine learning
authors: Karsten Walz Jensen, Mie Andersen, Raffaele Cheula
abstract: Dopants can tune the activity of zirconia-based CO$_2$ hydrogenation catalysts through changes in adsorbate and transition-state (TS) energetics. Computing these quantities with density functional theory (DFT) becomes expensive when several dopants, reaction intermediates, and TSs must be screened. Here, we further develop the graph-based machine learning method Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman Gaussian Process Regression (WWL-GPR): we introduce additional electronic-structure and local-environment features relevant for oxide surfaces and use the resulting model to predict adsorption and TS energies on ZrO$_2$(101) surfaces doped with Al$^{3+}$, Cd$^{2+}$, Ga$^{3+}$, In$^{3+}$, and Zn$^{2+}$. Adsorbate-surface structures are represented as attributed graphs that combine bonds connectivity and features. We benchmark WWL-GPR against thermodynamic scaling relations (TSR) for reaction intermediates and Bronsted-Evans-Polanyi relations (BEP) for TSs, and then propagate the predicted energies to microkinetic CH$_3$OH-yield estimates. WWL-GPR consistently improves the prediction of reaction intermediate energetics relative to linear scaling approaches and provides TS estimates that are competitive with BEP-based models. These improvements become especially relevant when the predicted energetics are propagated through the reaction network. Microkinetic calculations show that WWL-GPR-derived energies give CH$_3$OH yields closer to DFT-derived yields than the linear-relation workflow. Degree-of-rate-control analysis links the activity errors to dopant-dependent rate-controlling steps, including HCOO* formation, H$_2$COOH* dissociation, and H$_3$CO* formation. These results support WWL-GPR as a data-efficient surrogate for connecting atomistic energetics with catalyst-screening observables on doped oxide surfaces.

infographic.key_insight: Adding local electronic-structure and surface-environment features to WWL-GPR lets a graph-based model predict dopant-dependent adsorption and transition-state energies on ZrO2 surfaces more accurately than simple linear scaling rules.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a more data-efficient way to screen doped oxide catalysts and better estimate downstream CH3OH yield trends without running DFT for every intermediate and transition state.
method: Represent adsorbate-surface structures as attributed graphs.
Train WWL-GPR with added oxide-relevant electronic and local-environment descriptors.
Benchmark against TSR for intermediates and BEP for transition states, then propagate predictions through microkinetic modeling.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that WWL-GPR consistently improves intermediate energetics over scaling relations, yields competitive transition-state estimates versus BEP, and produces CH3OH yields closer to DFT-derived values after microkinetic propagation.
infographic.watch_item: Performance still depends on the quality and coverage of the training set, so extrapolation to new dopants, surfaces, or reaction conditions may be unreliable.
infographic.paper_title: Improved screening of doped ZrO$_2$ catalysts for CO$_2$ hydrogenation from graph-based machine learning

title: Ceramic Materials: From Atomic Bonding and Processing to Microstructure, Functional Properties, and Biomedical Applications
authors: Jairo Rondon, Juan Valera, Alex Velez Cruz, Irela Perez Magin
abstract: Ceramic materials are inorganic, predominantly nonmetallic solids whose performance is governed by the interplay among atomic bonding, crystal structure, processing, microstructure, and functional properties. Their ionic and covalent bonding provides high hardness, thermal and chemical stability, wear resistance, and diverse electrical behavior, but also limits plastic deformation and increases sensitivity to flaws, porosity, grain boundaries, and residual stresses. This review examines ceramics through the processing--microstructure--property--performance relationship, emphasizing the effects of crystal chemistry, defects, grain size, porosity, and phase stability on mechanical, thermal, electrical, and biological behavior. Conventional sintering, sol--gel processing, and additive manufacturing are discussed as key routes for controlling densification, porosity, geometry, and composition. Biomedical ceramics, including alumina, zirconia, calcium phosphates, hydroxyapatite, tricalcium phosphate, and bioactive glasses, are also reviewed. Emerging topics include nanoceramics, smart ceramics, composites, multimaterial manufacturing, defect engineering, immunomodulatory bioceramics, and sustainable processing. Major challenges remain in brittle fracture, processing heterogeneity, degradation control, scale-up, and the porosity--strength trade-off. Future advances will require integrating advanced manufacturing, multiscale characterization, predictive modeling, and data-driven design.

infographic.key_insight: Ceramic performance is controlled by the full processing–microstructure–property chain, where bonding, defects, porosity, grain size, and phase stability determine mechanical, thermal, electrical, and biological behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Better control of sintering, sol–gel routes, and additive manufacturing can improve densification, geometry, composition, and reliability for structural and biomedical ceramic components.
method: Conventional sintering for densification and microstructure control
Sol–gel processing for composition and phase tailoring
Additive manufacturing for complex geometry and multimaterial fabrication
infographic.evidence_signal: This is a review article synthesizing prior studies rather than reporting a new experimental dataset or model evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Brittle fracture and the porosity–strength trade-off remain major limitations, especially when scaling up or managing processing heterogeneity.
infographic.paper_title: Ceramic Materials: From Atomic Bonding and Processing to Microstructure, Functional Properties, and Biomedical Applications

title: $C_4$-Equivariant Flow Matching on Anisotropic Power-Diagram Graphs for Microstructure Generation
authors: Dawid Lipinski, Jixiang Qing, Henry Moss
abstract: Acquiring realistic microstructure data through Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) is costly and time consuming, often relying on specialised equipment. As microstructures strongly influence material properties, generating realistic samples is essential for modelling the behaviour of polycrystalline materials. We introduce a generative model for synthesising realistic polycrystalline microstructures using flow matching and graph neural networks. By representing microstructures as anisotropic power diagrams, our model learns a compact geometric parametrisation and can render generated samples at arbitrary pixel resolution. A $C_4$-equivariant architecture incorporates rotational symmetry directly into the model, ensuring that rotations of the input noise produce corresponding rotations of the generated microstructure. We also demonstrate how training-free guidance can be used to generate complex microstructures, based on user defined objective function. In particular, we generate microstructures resembling a copper weld, cast metal slab, 3D-printed stainless steel and heterogeneous lamella titanium.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a $C_4$-equivariant flow-matching generative model that learns polycrystalline microstructures as anisotropic power diagrams, enabling realistic synthesis at controllable resolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical way to generate synthetic microstructure data for materials design and property modeling when EBSD measurements are limited, costly, or time consuming.
method: Represents microstructures as anisotropic power-diagram graphs for a compact geometric encoding.
Trains a flow-matching graph neural network with $C_4$ rotational equivariance to preserve symmetry under 90° rotations.
Uses training-free guidance to steer generation toward target microstructure styles such as weld, cast, printed, and lamellar structures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports qualitative generation of several distinct real-world-like microstructure types and the ability to render samples at arbitrary pixel resolution.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is described mainly through generated examples in the abstract, so practical fidelity, diversity, and robustness will need validation on broader experimental datasets.
infographic.paper_title: $C_4$-Equivariant Flow Matching on Anisotropic Power-Diagram Graphs for Microstructure Generation

title: Drude, Where's My Charge? End-to-End Learning of Polarizable Drude Force Fields for Polymer Electrolytes
authors: Artur Lyssenko, KyuJung Jun, Rafael Gomez-Bombarelli
abstract: Molecular dynamics simulations of solid polymer electrolytes require force fields that are fast enough to converge ion transport over hundreds of nanoseconds, yet accurately describe the ion-polymer interactions that govern it. Fixed-charge force fields meet the first requirement but neglect electronic polarization, an effect often approximated by scaling ionic charges using empirically chosen factors. Here we present AutoDrude, a differentiable framework that parametrizes polarizable Drude force fields directly from DFT energies, forces, and dipoles, with no empirical tuning and at only 1.20 times the cost of a fixed-charge simulation. For PEO-LiTFSI, the dipole-constrained (hard-constraint) AutoDrude model reproduces the experimental ionic conductivity as accurately as the best charge-scaled model (17% versus 16% mean absolute percentage error). We compare the polarizable forcefield to fixed charge ones models by fitting a fixed charge model. Unlike the charge-scaled models tested here, however, AutoDrude also reproduces the dilute-limit cation transference number, its increase with salt concentration, and the absence of Li-TFSI contact ion pairs at low concentration. A penalty-based (soft-constraint) variant yields a closer fit to the DFT reference yet underestimates the conductivity by up to an order of magnitude, demonstrating that closer agreement with DFT training data alone does not guarantee accurate ion transport. These results indicate that although charge scaling can reproduce ionic conductivity the explicit inclusion of polarization is necessary to capture the concentration dependence of cation transport in PEO-LiTFSI.

infographic.key_insight: AutoDrude learns polarizable Drude force fields directly from DFT data and captures polymer-electrolyte ion transport more faithfully than fixed-charge or charge-scaled models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster molecular dynamics simulations of solid polymer electrolytes with near-experimental conductivity and better prediction of cation transport behavior.
method: Differentiable end-to-end parametrization of Drude force fields from DFT energies, forces, and dipoles
Hard-constraint and soft-constraint variants for matching target dipoles
Benchmarked on PEO-LiTFSI against fixed-charge and charge-scaled baselines
infographic.evidence_signal: For PEO-LiTFSI, the hard-constraint model matches experimental ionic conductivity with 17% mean absolute percentage error, comparable to the best charge-scaled model at 16%, while also reproducing transference number trends and low-concentration ion pairing behavior.
infographic.watch_item: The soft-constraint variant fits DFT data more closely but can underestimate conductivity by up to an order of magnitude, so lower training error does not guarantee correct transport predictions.
infographic.paper_title: Drude, Where's My Charge? End-to-End Learning of Polarizable Drude Force Fields for Polymer Electrolytes

title: Dynamic Chemical Changes of Ti3C2Tx MXenes in Halide Perovskite Precursor Environments
authors: Kirill Sobolev, Nagaprasad Reddy Samala, Mariela J. Pavan, Sharon Hazan, Vladimir Ezersky, Shakked Schwartz
abstract: The integration of two-dimensional Ti3C2Tx MXenes into Halide Perovskite (HaP) optoelectronics has shown immense potential for enhancing device performance, yet the fundamental chemical interactions within the precursor ink (a critical stage determining the final material state) remain largely unexplored. This study presents a comprehensive investigation into the chemical stability and surface evolution of Ti3C2Tx MXenes when exposed to the individual and combined components of a model methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) solution. By combining detailed X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) analysis with Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations, we decouple the complex interactions between MXenes and the ink constituents. We demonstrate that elemental iodine (I2) and polyiodides (In-) act as aggressive oxidizers, triggering rapid degradation and dissolution of the MXene flakes. Conversely, lead iodide (PbI2) induces a slower oxidation process driven by the strong adsorption of Pb2+ ions onto oxygen terminated sites. In stark contrast, methylammonium iodide (MAI) exhibits a stabilizing effect: it adsorbs onto the MXene surface via hydrogen bonding, effectively passivating the flakes and retarding degradation. In addition, our results reveal that the sequence of precursor addition governs the MXene surface state, requiring extra caution, but also enabling further tunability. These findings provide a critical view on how MXene integration with materials, in general, and HaP in particular, should be perceived, providing a fundamental for their rational engineering.

infographic.key_insight: In MAPbI3 precursor environments, Ti3C2Tx MXenes are chemically stabilized by MAI but rapidly degraded by I2/polyiodides and more slowly oxidized by PbI2, with precursor order strongly affecting surface evolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: MXene-enabled perovskite inks must be formulated and sequenced carefully to preserve flake integrity and tune interfacial chemistry for optoelectronic performance.
method: X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) tracked MXene surface chemistry after exposure to individual precursor components.
Density Functional Theory (DFT) explained adsorption and oxidation mechanisms at the MXene surface.
Comparative testing isolated the roles of I2/polyiodides, PbI2, and MAI in degradation or passivation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports combined XPS and DFT evidence showing rapid oxidative dissolution from iodine species, slower PbI2-driven oxidation, and MAI-induced surface passivation.
infographic.watch_item: Precursor addition order is a critical implementation variable; changing the sequence can alter MXene stability and should be controlled carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamic Chemical Changes of Ti3C2Tx MXenes in Halide Perovskite Precursor Environments

title: VN-GraphGG: von Neumann--Mullins--based graph grain growth simulation
authors: Yuntong Huang, Zhihao Li, Shuyang Dai, Chang Ma, Yang Xiang
abstract: Efficient simulations of grain growth are essential for investigating the process-structure-property relationships in polycrystalline materials. We introduce a two-dimensional von Neumann-Mullins-based graph grain growth simulation (VN-GraphGG), which couples the grain-scale kinetics with microstructure reconstruction. The polycrystalline microstructure is represented as a graph with grain and junction nodes. The grain-area evolution on the grain graph is governed by the von Neumann--Mullins (VN) law, while a graph neural network is trained to reconstruct the microstructure from the graph. This separation allows kinetic coefficients to be varied without retraining the neural reconstruction model. Topological changes during grain growth such as disappearance of grains and changes in neighbor relations are handled straightforwardly through reconstruction and postprocessing. Simulations demonstrate accurate predictions of VN kinetics and coarsening statistics, and significant speedup over the phase-field simulations. The proposed method provides a foundation for efficient grain growth simulation based on grain-scale kinetics, opening the way to incorporate a broader range of physical mechanisms. An application example is presented for abnormal grain growth, in which kinetic heterogeneity significantly influences the grain microstructure evolution.

infographic.key_insight: VN-GraphGG separates grain-growth kinetics from microstructure reconstruction, using the von Neumann–Mullins law on a graph and a GNN to rebuild the evolving polycrystal.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster two-dimensional grain-growth simulation with adjustable kinetic coefficients, supporting efficient studies of process-structure-property relationships in materials.
method: Represent the polycrystalline microstructure as a graph with grain nodes and junction nodes.
Evolve grain areas with the von Neumann–Mullins law on the grain graph.
Use a graph neural network to reconstruct microstructure and handle topology changes via reconstruction/postprocessing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accurate prediction of VN kinetics and coarsening statistics, plus significant speedup compared with phase-field simulations, including an abnormal grain-growth example.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is presented for two-dimensional grain growth, so extension to more complex 3D microstructures and robustness to strong heterogeneity may require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: VN-GraphGG: von Neumann--Mullins--based graph grain growth simulation

title: Specialized machine learning force fields for materials dynamics
authors: Yue Wu, Haoyu Wan, Yuan Tian, Deng Pan, Mingwei Chen
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are transforming atomistic simulations by accessing unprecedented length and time scales. While pretrained equivariant graph neural networks achieve robust zero-shot performance for near-equilibrium properties across broad chemical spaces, their translation to complex materials dynamics remains fundamentally challenged by out-of-distribution reactive states, representation biases, and computational scaling limits. In this Review, we examine how physics-driven specialization extends the applicability of MLIPs to complex dynamical systems. We systematically evaluate the structural trade-offs in MLIP design: the undersampling of highly strained configurations, the prohibitive computational overhead of high-order message-passing architectures, and the necessity of nonlocal interactions for open and field-coupled systems. Through four demanding application contexts - electrified interfaces, compositionally fluctuating open systems, multiphase evolution, and large-scale fracture - we establish a framework for observable-specific validation. Highlighting the complementary roles of universal foundation models and task-specific potentials, we emphasize that targeted adaptations must be rigorously benchmarked against intended observables. We conclude with a roadmap for developing physically consistent, hardware-aware force fields that seamlessly connect electronic-structure accuracy to macroscopic materials phenomena.

infographic.key_insight: Specialized, physics-driven machine learning force fields are needed to accurately simulate complex materials dynamics beyond the near-equilibrium regime where universal models are strongest.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For atomistic modeling of interfaces, open systems, phase evolution, and fracture, the right force field must be chosen and validated against the specific observable of interest, not just general benchmark accuracy.
method: Review and compare design trade-offs in ML interatomic potentials
Assess four challenging use cases: electrified interfaces, open systems, multiphase evolution, and fracture
Emphasize observable-specific benchmarking and hardware-aware model design
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper synthesizes findings from demanding application contexts and benchmarks them against intended observables to show where pretrained equivariant models fail under out-of-distribution dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: High-order or overly general architectures can be computationally expensive and still miss reactive or nonlocal physics, so specialization may improve accuracy but can reduce transferability.
infographic.paper_title: Specialized machine learning force fields for materials dynamics

title: Zatom-2: Multitask Pretraining on Atomistic Data for Generative Modeling across Domains
authors: Miruna Cretu, Alex Abrudan, Antonia Panescu, Tynan Perez, Rishabh Anand, N. Benjamin Erichson
abstract: Unified atomistic modeling has the potential to accelerate discovery in chemistry, materials science, and biology by bridging data-rich chemical domains and data-scarce biological contexts. However, existing generative approaches to atomistic modeling remain highly specialized to scientific disciplines (chemistry vs. biology) or do not leverage both high-volume organic (molecule) and inorganic (material) data for general-purpose pretraining. To this end, we introduce Zatom-2, an atomistic generative model pretrained on approximately five million structures from the OMol25 and OMat24 electronic structure datasets. Zatom-2 features a multiscale Transformer architecture coupled with conditional flow matching that supports force conditioning and foundational pretraining tasks such as generation, structure prediction, and prediction of molecular and material energies and forces. Empirically, Zatom-2 achieves better molecular distribution fidelity than Zatom-1 and achieves strong performance on existing molecule and material generation benchmarks. Zatom-2 demonstrates the ability to control sample generation across low- and high-force regimes, and enhances protein generation in a low-data setting through joint generative-predictive pretraining and transfer learning, increasing protein backbone designability in a length extrapolation setting from 67.8% without pretraining to 74.8% after finetuning on 2,000 protein domains.

infographic.key_insight: Zatom-2 is a unified atomistic generative foundation model that pretrains on both molecular and material data to improve generation, prediction, and cross-domain transfer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for computational materials and molecular design because a single pretrained model can support structure generation, property prediction, and force-conditioned sampling across chemistry, materials, and biology.
method: Pretrained on ~5 million structures from OMol25 and OMat24
Uses a multiscale Transformer with conditional flow matching
Supports generation, structure prediction, and energy/force prediction with force conditioning
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved molecular distribution fidelity over Zatom-1, strong benchmark performance, controllable low- and high-force generation, and protein backbone designability rising from 67.8% to 74.8% after finetuning on 2,000 protein domains.
infographic.watch_item: The model’s broad performance may depend on large-scale high-quality pretraining data, so transfer to new domains or low-data settings may still require careful finetuning and validation.
infographic.paper_title: Zatom-2: Multitask Pretraining on Atomistic Data for Generative Modeling across Domains

title: X-ray absorption spectroscopic studies of oxygen-deficient double perovskite oxide NdBaCo$_2$O$_{5+δ}$ ($δ\sim 0.65$)
authors: Himanshu Pant, S. Khalid, R. Bindu
abstract: The degree of oxygen vacancy in A-site-doped layered double perovskite oxides can lead to anion vacancy ordering, which subsequently results in distinct superstructures. We have studied oxygen deficient double perovskite oxide, NdBaCo$2$O$_{5+δ}$ ($δ\sim$ 0.65), utilising X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy complemented by multiple scattering and first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT+U). The present results establish a direct correlation between oxygen-vacancy distribution, magnetic inhomogeneity, and charge transport in layered cobaltates. Our investigations on the Co K, Ba, and Nd $L_{\mathrm{III}}$ edges suggest that the near-edge spectra, based on the number and shape of the spectral features, indicate the value of $δ$ for the compound under study lies closer to 0.75. The analysis of the Ba $L_{\mathrm{III}}$ edge spectrum confirms the +2 oxidation state for Ba ions. The Co K-edge near-edge spectra suggest the possibility of oxygen vacancies arising at the basal sites in addition to the apical sites. This is counterintuitive to the common understanding that oxygen vacancies usually occur at the apical sites, i.e., in the lanthanide (Nd) layer in these compounds. Such a distribution of oxygen vacancies naturally explains the Griffith phase and the conduction mechanism of variable range hopping observed in the compound. The vacancy distribution, when at the optimum level, can also bring about easier oxygen ion mobility and a more sensitive and faster oxygen sensor. We believe that our results will help in tailoring oxygen-ion mobility and enhancing oxygen-sensing performance.

infographic.key_insight: XANES and DFT+U indicate that oxygen vacancies in NdBaCo2O5+δ are distributed beyond the usual apical sites, helping explain the compound’s magnetic inhomogeneity and variable-range-hopping transport.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling vacancy ordering in layered cobaltates could improve oxygen-ion mobility and enable faster, more sensitive oxygen-sensing materials.
method: Co K-edge, Ba LIII-edge, and Nd LIII-edge XANES analysis
Multiple-scattering simulations of near-edge spectra
DFT+U-based first-principles modeling of vacancy distribution
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that spectral features from the XANES data suggest δ is closer to 0.75 than the nominal ~0.65, and confirm Ba remains in the +2 oxidation state.
infographic.watch_item: The vacancy-site assignment is inferred from spectroscopy and modeling, so direct structural validation of the oxygen-vacancy distribution would strengthen the conclusion.
infographic.paper_title: X-ray absorption spectroscopic studies of oxygen-deficient double perovskite oxide NdBaCo$_2$O$_{5+δ}$ ($δ\sim 0.65$)

title: Role of composition-tuned disorder on magnetic exchange interactions in NiRuMnGa
authors: Manikantha Panda, Prabuddha Kant Mishra, Vinod Kumar, Wilfrid Prellier, Rahul Sharma, Tapas Paramanik
abstract: We report the experimental investigation of the quaternary Heusler alloy NiRuMnGa, complemented by first-principles calculations. The energetically favorable crystal structure was identified from first-principles calculations and subsequently used as the structural model for refinement of the powder X-ray diffraction data. The refinement shows good agreement with the experimental pattern and reveals substantial B2-type disorder involving Ni/Ru and Mn/Ga site intermixing. The dc magnetic response exhibits pronounced ZFC--FC irreversibility near $\sim 48$ K, with the irreversibility temperature shifting toward lower temperatures under increasing magnetic field, indicating a field-sensitive glassy state. The isothermal magnetization remains unsaturated up to 7 T, reaching only $\sim 0.4\,μ_{\mathrm{B}}$/f.u., accompanied by pronounced hysteresis, suggesting competing exchange interactions and frustrated magnetic moments. AC susceptibility, together with magnetic relaxation and memory measurements, confirms slow spin dynamics characteristic of a cluster glass state. The lack of a discernible heat-capacity anomaly near the irreversibility temperature further supports the absence of conventional long-range magnetic order. Collectively, these results demonstrate that competition between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions in NiRuMnGa leads to magnetic frustration and stabilizes a cluster glass state.

infographic.key_insight: Composition-tuned site disorder in quaternary Heusler NiRuMnGa frustrates magnetic exchange, stabilizing a cluster-glass state instead of long-range magnetic order.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This shows how controlled antisite disorder in Heusler alloys can be used to tune low-temperature magnetic behavior, which is relevant for functional magnetic materials and spintronic design.
method: First-principles calculations to identify the energetically favorable crystal structure.
Powder X-ray diffraction refinement using the computed structure as the model.
Magnetic characterization via dc/AC susceptibility, hysteresis, relaxation, and memory measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports B2-type Ni/Ru and Mn/Ga disorder, ZFC-FC irreversibility near 48 K that shifts with field, unsaturated magnetization up to 7 T, and no heat-capacity anomaly near the transition.
infographic.watch_item: Because the magnetic response is strongly disorder-dependent, the inferred cluster-glass state may vary with composition, sample homogeneity, and degree of antisite mixing.
infographic.paper_title: Role of composition-tuned disorder on magnetic exchange interactions in NiRuMnGa

title: Resolving the interfacial mechanical landscape of monolayer NbSe2 grown by confined epitaxy
authors: Ye Wang
abstract: Confined epitaxy has recently emerged as a novel methodology for controlled growth of high-quality monolayer two-dimensional (2D) materials. However, mechanistic understanding remains limited to analysing nucleus adsorption and diffusion barriers. Here, I discover that van der Waals (vdW) confinement not only affects the specific adsorption and diffusion of nuclei on confined substrates but also induces strong coupling to atomic forces at the interface. Using artificial intelligence (AI) assisted density functional theory (DFT) calculations, I study how vdW confinement couples to the atomic motion of monolayer NbSe2 grown between c-plane sapphire and hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN). The calculated force-electronic landscape yields large mechanical forces of +0.070 and -0.04 eV per Angstrom on Nb and Se, respectively, giving rise to a unit-cell interfacial interaction energy up to 2.4 eV, comparable to reported adsorption and diffusion energies on similar substrates. The results indicate that interfacial mechanics may explain the success of confined epitaxy. The findings suggest that tuning interfacial mechanics, and related vdW mechanochemistry, could be a promising route to high-throughput, high-quality materials synthesis.

infographic.key_insight: vdW confinement in confined epitaxy does more than steer adsorption and diffusion; it generates strong interfacial forces that mechanically couple to monolayer NbSe2 growth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineering the interfacial mechanical landscape could improve high-throughput synthesis of high-quality 2D materials grown by confined epitaxy.
method: AI-assisted DFT calculations of monolayer NbSe2 growth between c-plane sapphire and h-BN
Computed force-electronic landscape at the interface to quantify atomic forces
Compared interfacial interaction energy with reported adsorption and diffusion energies
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports large calculated forces of +0.070 and -0.04 eV/Å on Nb and Se and a unit-cell interfacial interaction energy up to 2.4 eV, indicating a strong mechanical contribution.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusion is based on computational modeling, so experimental validation is still needed before using interfacial mechanics as a design rule for growth.
infographic.paper_title: Resolving the interfacial mechanical landscape of monolayer NbSe2 grown by confined epitaxy

title: Accelerating dynamic polarizability calculations of organic molecules using equivariant graph neural networks
authors: Houssam Metni, Maria Kraus, Marie Louise Schubert, Marjan Krstic, Carsten Rockstuhl, Pascal Friederich
abstract: Predicting the dynamic polarizability tensor of organic molecules is essential for simulating light-matter interactions in optoelectronic devices, yet conventional quantum-chemical methods such as time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) are computationally expensive and limit large-scale screening. We present an equivariant graph neural network architecture that predicts frequency-dependent, complex-valued dynamic polarizability tensors directly from readily available molecular information, such as 3D geometry and UV-vis spectra. The model learns to approximate the shape and magnitude of the dynamic polarizability tensor, capturing both dispersive and absorptive features that define the molecular optical response. We evaluate the model on molecules from both the QM9 dataset and the Harvard organic photovoltaic dataset using various metrics, including the earth mover's distance, which is suitable for comparing spectral quantities. For both datasets, the model successfully reproduces the main features of the dynamic polarizability tensor and generalizes across diverse molecules. To assess the applicability, we further validated the model using a downstream workflow to calculate the optical properties of organic photovoltaic devices. We used the model-predicted polarizabilities to perform device-level optical simulations, yielding charge carrier generation rates in agreement with TD-DFT-based results ($R^2 = 0.94$). Our approach offers a promising complement, or even an alternative, to conventional methods such as TD-DFT, enabling faster and more efficient screening of photoactive organic molecules for optoelectronic applications.

infographic.key_insight: An equivariant graph neural network can predict frequency-dependent complex dynamic polarizability tensors of organic molecules directly from molecular structure and spectra, closely matching TD-DFT behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables much faster screening of photoactive molecules for optoelectronic device design by replacing many expensive quantum-chemical polarizability calculations with a learned surrogate.
method: Uses an equivariant GNN to respect molecular geometry and tensor symmetries.
Inputs readily available information such as 3D structure and UV-vis spectra.
Predicts complex-valued, frequency-resolved polarizability tensors for downstream optical simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was tested on QM9 and Harvard organic photovoltaic molecules, reproduced main polarizability features, and achieved device-level charge-carrier generation rates that agreed with TD-DFT results with R² = 0.94.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on training-set coverage and the quality of available molecular geometries/spectra, so out-of-distribution chemistries or device conditions could reduce reliability.
infographic.paper_title: Accelerating dynamic polarizability calculations of organic molecules using equivariant graph neural networks

title: Necessary conditions for benchmarking next-generation AI in materials discovery
authors: Daniel E Widdowson, Tatiana V Kurlina, Olga D Anosova, Vitaliy A Kurlin
abstract: Current AI predicts materials by speeding up energy minimisation and training on large databases. However, scaling data generation prevents manual analysis by domain experts. If novelty is evaluated by chemical compositions or traditional representations in Crystallographic Information Files, or standard structure matchers based on manually chosen thresholds, one can easily generate millions of ``new'' compositions or files without discovering truly novel materials. This paper uses a hierarchy of crystal invariants to continuously trace and quantify structural novelty based on the new mathematical definition of a crystal structure and asymptotic guarantees for invariant descriptors. The invariant-based analysis through cascade computations on a modest computer exposes the unexpected scale of duplication in the world's largest materials databases, shown here in the high-profile case of GNoME datasets. To prevent current ``embarrassment of over-prediction'', we propose necessary conditions for next-generation AI that should be automatically enforced before claiming any new materials.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that counting novel compositions or CIFs can massively overstate discovery, and that crystal-invariant hierarchies are needed to verify true structural novelty.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For materials-AI pipelines, the result implies benchmarking must include automatic novelty checks and duplicate detection before any candidate is claimed as a new material.
method: Defines a new mathematical notion of crystal structure.
Uses a hierarchy of crystal invariants to trace and quantify structural novelty continuously.
Applies cascade computations with asymptotic guarantees to detect duplication in large databases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that invariant-based analysis on a modest computer revealed unexpectedly large duplication in major materials databases, including the GNoME datasets.
infographic.watch_item: Novelty claims still depend on how invariant thresholds and database matching rules are implemented, so poor choices can under- or over-count distinct structures.
infographic.paper_title: Necessary conditions for benchmarking next-generation AI in materials discovery

title: Dislocation mediated twin boundary faceting in $β$-Sn
authors: John Israel, Ian Chesser, Khanh Dang, Vinamra Agrawal
abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs), including twin boundaries (TBs), play a critical role in plastic deformation by interacting with dislocations. The deformation and strengthening mechanisms in $β$-Sn are of significant interest because Sn-based alloys are widely used as solder materials. Recent experiments have shown deformation-induced faceting in $β$-Sn arising from twin-dislocation interactions. Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations informed by a recently developed machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP), we demonstrate a $\langle c\rangle$ dislocation-absorption mediated faceting reaction along $(301)$ TBs in $β$-Sn in which facet length grows with the number of absorbed dislocations. We show that the predicted facet length is consistent with isotropic elasticity theory only when the disclination character of the asymmetric twin facet is taken into account. We discuss analogies to faceting reactions in other low symmetry metals and hypothesize that the ubiquity of $(301)$ twins in $β$-Sn stems from their ability to grow rapidly through a forest of dislocation obstacles.

infographic.key_insight: In β-Sn, twin-boundary faceting on (301) twins is driven by absorption of <c> dislocations, with facet length increasing as more dislocations are absorbed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This mechanism helps explain and potentially control deformation and strengthening in Sn-based solder alloys, especially under dislocation-rich loading conditions.
method: Molecular dynamics simulations of β-Sn twin-boundary behavior
Use of a machine-learned interatomic potential trained for the material
Comparison against isotropic elasticity theory including disclination effects
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulation results showing a dislocation-absorption-mediated faceting reaction and that the predicted facet length matches elasticity theory only when disclination character is included.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism is inferred from simulation and theory for a specific boundary orientation, so broader applicability to other loading paths or microstructures should be validated experimentally.
infographic.paper_title: Dislocation mediated twin boundary faceting in $β$-Sn

title: Bottom-Up Prediction of Amorphous Poly(1,3-dioxolane) using Ab Initio Reactive Machine-Learning Force Fields
authors: Yizhi Song, Bharatha K. Gunawardana, Kriti Alam, Teresa Shah, Deepa Ranabhat, Hsin-Yu Ko
abstract: Poly(1,3-dioxolane) (pDXL) is a chemically recyclable polyether that can be synthesized by living cationic ring-opening polymerization with precise control of chain length into the ultra-high-molecular-weight (UHMW) regime, where it acquires enhanced mechanical properties. Like most polymers, however, it has amorphous condensed-phase structure, and diffraction measurements alone cannot resolve the atomistic microstructure that underlies them. In this work, we predict the ensemble of the pDXL microstructures by applying a recently developed AI-accelerated ab initio bottom-up polymer structure prediction (AI$^{2}$-BPSP) framework that simulates the living polymerization of pDXL under experimental synthetic conditions with machine-learning force fields trained within van der Waals-corrected hybrid density functional theory. Partitioning the predicted X-ray and neutron diffraction signal between the growing chain and the surrounding monomer resolves its dominant feature into two counteracting modes: a monomer contribution near $q \approx 1.5$ Å$^{-1}$ that decays as monomer is consumed, and a polymer contribution near $q \approx 1.6$ Å$^{-1}$ that is absent in oligomers and grows with chain length. This work paves the way to direct accuracy validation of these statistically significant, first-principles, and chain-length resolved diffraction predictions against experiments.

infographic.key_insight: AI-accelerated bottom-up simulations reveal that amorphous pDXL diffraction is governed by two competing structural signals: a monomer peak that fades during polymerization and a polymer peak that emerges with chain growth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables first-principles, chain-length-resolved prediction of amorphous polymer microstructure, helping link synthesis conditions to properties in chemically recyclable UHMW polyether materials.
method: AI2-BPSP bottom-up polymerization simulation under experimental conditions
Machine-learning force fields trained on van der Waals-corrected hybrid DFT
Partitioned X-ray and neutron diffraction into monomer vs. growing-chain contributions
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports statistically significant, chain-length-resolved diffraction predictions with distinct features near q ≈ 1.5 Å⁻¹ for monomer and q ≈ 1.6 Å⁻¹ for polymer.
infographic.watch_item: The predictions still require direct experimental validation, and the accuracy depends on transferability of the ML force fields to the amorphous condensed-phase polymerization regime.
infographic.paper_title: Bottom-Up Prediction of Amorphous Poly(1,3-dioxolane) using Ab Initio Reactive Machine-Learning Force Fields

title: Provenance-grouped protocol for evaluating machine learning in perovskite photovoltaics
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou
abstract: Machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells are typically evaluated using random data splits, which we show systematically leak information through massive internal duplication. Because nearly two-thirds of curated devices share their exact recipe with another, random splits primarily reward the mere recall of historical data rather than testing true physical generalisation. To solve this, we mapped the institutional provenance of the Perovskite Database and established a rigorous hierarchy of grouped splits that progressively isolate duplicate devices, publications, and institutions. Benchmarking thirteen models establishes new state-of-the-art performance across all splits and reveals a critical regime shift: while tree ensembles dominate random splits by recognising familiar recipes, their ranking collapses on genuinely unseen institutions and future discoveries, where composition-aware neural architectures excel. Furthermore, feature importance demonstrates that the device architecture and fabrication methodology dictate final efficiency just as strongly as the absorber chemistry. This standardised protocol empowers the community to separate memorisation from true physical discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Random train/test splits in perovskite-ML benchmarks can massively overestimate performance because duplicated recipes leak across the split, so provenance-grouped evaluation is needed to measure real generalization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For data-driven perovskite device design, this protocol helps researchers choose models and compare results on truly unseen materials, publications, and institutions rather than on memorized historical recipes.
method: Mapped institutional provenance in the Perovskite Database.
Built a hierarchy of grouped splits that separate duplicate devices, papers, and institutions.
Benchmarked 13 models across progressively harder evaluation regimes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Nearly two-thirds of curated devices share an exact recipe with another, making random splits a weak test of physical discovery; performance rankings change sharply when moving to unseen institutions and future data.
infographic.watch_item: Grouped splits are stricter and more realistic, but they can reduce apparent benchmark scores and require careful provenance curation to avoid misclassification.
infographic.paper_title: Provenance-grouped protocol for evaluating machine learning in perovskite photovoltaics

title: Doubly Metastable Synthesis for Accelerated Quantum Materials Discovery
authors: Kyuho Lee, Berit H. Goodge, Soonhyun Kwon, Yash Anand, Theo Manev, Maximilien F. Debbas
abstract: New physics emerges from new materials, which in turn rely on the development of new synthesis techniques. Identifying the enlargement of metastable synthesis window as enabling for realizing novel materials, we develop diffusion-activated epitaxy, a technique which combines two metastable synthesis methods of diffusion and epitaxy. We observe that within a narrow window of investigated synthesis space we can experimentally identify the stabilization of four distinct phases, three of which show X-ray diffraction and scanning transmission electron microscopy characterization data that are incompatible with the crystal structures registered in experimental and computational inorganic structure databases. These results suggest an enlarged metastable synthesis window is enabled by this synthesis approach, identifying doubly metastable synthesis as a promising method for exploration of quantum materials.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces diffusion-activated epitaxy, a doubly metastable synthesis strategy that enlarges the accessible metastable window and enables discovery of previously inaccessible crystal phases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach could accelerate quantum materials discovery by making novel, metastable compounds experimentally accessible through a combined diffusion-and-epitaxy route.
method: Combine two metastable synthesis modes: diffusion and epitaxy.
Systematically explore a narrow synthesis space to stabilize new phases.
Validate products with X-ray diffraction and scanning transmission electron microscopy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Within a narrow region of synthesis conditions, the authors stabilized four distinct phases, and three showed XRD/STEM signatures inconsistent with structures in existing experimental and computational databases.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstrated phase discovery occurs in a narrow investigated synthesis window, so broader reproducibility and scalability still need confirmation.
infographic.paper_title: Doubly Metastable Synthesis for Accelerated Quantum Materials Discovery

title: Variational neural transport for aggregation-diffusion equations
authors: Qianyi Li, Hailiang Liu
abstract: We develop a neural transport framework for nonlinear, nonlocal aggregationdiffusion equations arising in chemotaxis, polymer dynamics, and related applications. Based on the Onsager variational principle, we reformulate the governing equation as a constrained optimal control problem, taking the velocity field as the control and evolving the density via the associated continuity equation. The velocity field is parameterized by a neural network trained on the variational objective evaluated along particle trajectories. By coupling the density and generalized score equations into a single system solved via the Euler method, the score function propagates efficiently for loss evaluation. Furthermore, we establish a rigorous error analysis that decomposes the total error into approximation, optimization, Monte Carlo sampling, and time-discretization components, and prove corresponding error bounds. Numerical experiments across several representative models demonstrate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed approach.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns aggregation-diffusion PDEs into a variational optimal-control problem and learns a neural velocity field to transport densities while respecting the underlying physics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a physics-informed surrogate for complex transport-driven materials and biological dynamics, enabling faster simulation of nonlocal nonlinear density evolution.
method: Reformulate the PDE using the Onsager variational principle with velocity as the control variable.
Evolve the density with a continuity equation along particle trajectories and train a neural network on the variational objective.
Couple density and generalized score equations, then use Euler time stepping for efficient loss evaluation and error analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments on several representative models, showing accuracy and effectiveness, alongside a theoretical error decomposition and bounds.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the quality of time discretization, Monte Carlo sampling, and neural approximation, so stability and generalization should be checked carefully in new regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Variational neural transport for aggregation-diffusion equations

title: Predictive Synthesis of MOFs and COFs
authors: Bin Feng, Reid A. Coyle, Shyam Chand Pal, Peter Walther, Saeun Park, Zhiling Zheng
abstract: Predictive synthesis concerns the prospective modeling of how a targeted structure can be realized. The synthesis of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent organic frameworks (COFs) intrinsically involves a multidimensional space of interdependent variables, posing a challenge for bench chemists to parameterize and predict. In this Perspective, we discuss the evolution from chemical-intuition-driven experimentation toward the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in the laboratory. By virtue of prior knowledge, uncertainty, and experimental failure in determining what should be attempted next, we envision predictive synthesis progressing from static recipe recommendation toward real-time control and transferable principles of framework formation. In this context, the significance lies in transforming trial-and-error practice into a means of measurable chemical reasoning, thereby accelerating crystalline materials discovery and advancing synthetic chemistry.

infographic.key_insight: Predictive synthesis for MOFs and COFs aims to replace intuition-based trial-and-error with AI/ML-guided planning, moving toward real-time, transferable control of framework formation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, more reliable discovery and optimization of porous crystalline materials by turning complex synthesis variables into actionable experimental decisions.
method: Survey the evolution from empirical synthesis to AI/ML-assisted laboratory workflows.
Frame MOF/COF synthesis as a multidimensional prediction problem with interdependent variables.
Envision progression from static recipe recommendation to real-time control and generalizable formation principles.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract is a Perspective, so its evidence is conceptual and field-synthesizing rather than reporting new experimental benchmark data.
infographic.watch_item: Practical deployment may be limited by sparse, noisy synthesis data and the difficulty of transferring learned rules across different framework chemistries and lab conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Predictive Synthesis of MOFs and COFs

title: Deep learning driven framework for optimization of polycrystalline microstructures under competing strength requirements
authors: Ashwini Gupta, Indrashish Saha, Lori Graham-Brady, Tamer A. Zaki
abstract: Computational design of polycrystalline microstructures for enhanced mechanical performance requires repeated high-fidelity simulations over stochastic morphologies, rendering conventional crystal plasticity finite element (CPFE) approaches prohibitively expensive for optimization. Here, we develop a deep learning-driven framework for optimizing polycrystalline microstructures under competing quasi-static and dynamic performance requirements. A 3D U-Net surrogate maps polycrystalline copper microstructures directly to full-field velocity histories from plate-impact simulations, preserving the spatial and temporal resolution needed to evaluate dynamic performance and interrogate underlying wave interactions and failure mechanisms. The surrogate is coupled with stochastic microstructure generation and derivative-free optimization to efficiently navigate the design space. To monitor surrogate reliability during optimization, we introduce a distribution-consistent reliability region (DCRR) based on maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to quantify distributional shift from the training data. The framework is demonstrated for multiple design problems, including constrained optimization of spall and yield strengths and inverse design. The optimal designs are validated using CPFE simulations with less than 3% prediction error across all optimization cases, while the surrogate-driven optimization reduces cumulative evaluation time by approximately four orders of magnitude compared with direct CPFE-based optimization. Although demonstrated here for the design of polycrystalline microstructures targeting spall and yield strengths, the framework is broadly applicable to optimization problems where high-fidelity full-field simulations are prohibitively expensive but spatially and temporally resolved response information is essential for evaluating, interpreting, and optimizing candidate designs.

infographic.key_insight: A deep-learning surrogate can replace expensive crystal plasticity simulations to optimize polycrystalline microstructures while balancing competing strength targets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables practical, high-fidelity microstructure design for materials engineering by making multi-objective optimization of spall and yield strength computationally feasible.
method: Train a 3D U-Net to map 3D polycrystalline copper microstructures to full-field plate-impact velocity histories.
Couple the surrogate with stochastic microstructure generation and derivative-free optimization to search the design space.
Use a distribution-consistent reliability region (DCRR) based on MMD to track out-of-distribution risk during optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple optimization cases, CPFE validation showed less than 3% prediction error and the surrogate-driven workflow cut cumulative evaluation time by about four orders of magnitude.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on staying within the training-data distribution, so surrogate reliability must be monitored carefully when exploring new microstructure regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Deep learning driven framework for optimization of polycrystalline microstructures under competing strength requirements
